● SC had no jurisdiction over the election of the Senate President because the 1935 Constitution grants to the Senate the power to elect its own president, and thus, such matter is an internal matter that the Court is not allowed to delve into with respect to the doctrine of the separation of powers.
● When the 1935 Constitution declared that a majority of “each House” shall constitute a quorum, it did not mean “all” the members. Even a majority of all the members present constitute “the House.” Therefore, an absolute majority (12) of all senators less one (23) constitutes constitutional majority of the Senate for purposes of a quorum.
● Quorum Calculation Based on Active Membership: The Court ruled that a constitutional quorum is determined based on the active members of the chamber who are within the country and capable of participating, rather than a rigid count of the total statutory membership. - The Court ruled that senators who are outside the country or beyond the Senate's coercive physical jurisdiction are not functionally available or compellable by the Sergeant-at-Arms. Thus, they do not count for quorum calculation.
● The Court held that the walkout of the 10 senators did not prevent the remaining 12 from continuing the session and passing the resolution unanimously. The answer might be different had the resolution been approved only by ten or less (since it would need a quorum)
